blocks.html:
⚠️ Closed alpha — provisional docs. OpenDefence on Kubernetes (opendefence-platform) is in closed alpha and under rapid, breaking development. This page describes a moving target and will most likely be superseded by the documentation that ships with the first public release — treat everything here as provisional, and do not rely on it for a production deployment.

This page explains how the pvarki/opendefence-platform repository assembles into a running cluster: the Kustomize layout, the phased apply with readiness gates, the two target environments (local kind, cloud k3s packaged with Zarf), and how releases are versioned. It is for developers and operators who need to understand why the deploy works the way it does — the step-by-step install itself lives in Deploy on Kubernetes.

Repository layout

Everything Kubernetes lives under k8s/. Each component follows the same pattern:

k8s/<component>/
  base/                  # environment-agnostic manifests
  overlays/
    local/               # kind: image pins, local Certificates, IngressRoutes, TLSOptions
    cloud/               # k3s: same, plus ###ZARF_VAR_OPENDEFENCE_HOST### tokens

Components include the infrastructure operators (cert-manager, cloudnative-pg, external-secrets-operator, traefik, prometheus-operator, grafana-operator, trust-manager, linkerd), the monitoring pieces (monitoring-loki, monitoring-alloy, monitoring-grafana, …), opendefence-pki, the core opendefence-system, and one app-* directory per product (app-battlelog, app-tak, app-mtx, app-matrix).

Three reusable Kustomize Components sit in k8s/_shared/:

Component What it injects Used by
rmapi-container-init a container-init.sh ConfigMap that loads the internal CA bundle into OS trust stores at container start (self-described in-repo as a hack) opendefence-system/base
java-memory-tuning a jvm-memory-config for JVM heap sizing opendefence-system/base, app-tak/base
traefik-secret-mirror ServiceAccount + SecretStore + ExternalSecret that mirror the callsign-validity shared secret from opendefence-system into traefik-system k8s/main/<env>/infra-phase2

Nothing is applied per component, though. The deployable units are the phase entry points under k8s/main/<env>/<phase>/kustomization.yaml, where <env> is local or cloud and the phases (in order) are infra-phase1, infra-phase2, infra-phase3, monitoring, opendefence, opendefence-apps. Each phase kustomization just aggregates the right overlay of each component it owns. The diagram below traces one entry point — k8s/main/local/opendefence — down to what it actually composes:

blocks.html:
Two cloud-only quirks are worth knowing:

  • k8s/main/cloud/infra-phase1/bundles/ splits phase 1 into one kustomization per operator (cert-manager, cloudnative-pg, external-secrets-operator, grafana-operator, prometheus-operator, prometheus-operator-crds, traefik). The Zarf build renders each bundle into its own manifest file so that each generated Helm release stays under Kubernetes' Secret size limit (Zarf applies each manifest set as an internal Helm release, whose record lives in a single Secret — a one-shot render of all the CRD-heavy phase-1 operators would blow past it). The plain deploy:cloud path still renders infra-phase1 as one unit.
  • The cloud phase entry points carry JSON patches that strip Helm ownership labels/annotations (app.kubernetes.io/managed-by=Helm, helm.sh/chart, release-name annotations) from the rendered output, so Zarf-applied resources don't masquerade as Helm releases.

Tool versions are pinned in mise.toml: kubectl 1.36, kustomize 5.8.1, kind 0.31, zarf 0.76.0, linkerd stable-2.14.10, helm 3, task 3, cosign 3, among others. Helm is only ever invoked through Kustomize's helmCharts support — the task deploy path creates no Helm releases in the cluster.

Phase gating

Deployment is driven by taskfile.yaml. Both environments funnel into the same internal task, deploy:_apply, which for every phase runs:
kubectl kustomize --enable-helm k8s/main/<env>/<phase> | kubectl apply --server-side -f -

and then blocks on kubectl rollout status for specific deployments before the next phase is applied. The gates are not decorative — each one exists because the next phase submits resources the gated component must be ready to admit or act on:

After phase Waits on (rollout status) Why
infra-phase1 cnpg-controller-manager (ns cnpg-system), cert-manager-webhook (ns cert-manager), external-secrets-operator and external-secrets-operator-webhook (ns external-secrets-system), each 180s later phases submit Certificate, Bundle, ExternalSecret and CNPG Cluster custom resources; the CRDs and admission webhooks must be serving or those applies are rejected
infra-phase2 trust-manager (ns cert-manager), 180s phase 3's PKI publishes the CA chain through a trust-manager Bundle; trust-manager must be running to sync ca-bundle into every namespace
infra-phase3 linkerd-proxy-injector, linkerd-identity, linkerd-destination (ns linkerd), each 180s every meshed workload created afterwards must get its sidecar injected at pod creation; if the injector comes up late, core and product pods start unmeshed
monitoring no gate operator/instance split: the operators and CRDs went in phase 1, this phase only creates CR instances (Prometheus, Alertmanager, Grafana, Loki, Alloy)
opendefence deployment/rmapi 180s, deployment/keycloak 300s (ns opendefence-system) the product apps register against rmapi and authenticate through Keycloak on startup; applying them earlier just produces crash-looping pods
opendefence-apps applied last, nothing after it app-battlelog, app-tak, app-mtx, app-matrix consume everything above

blocks.html:
One known cross-phase subtlety: Traefik (phase 1) references the mirrored callsign-validity secret as a required env var, the mirror machinery lands in phase 2, but the source secret is only generated in the opendefence phase. The stack converges anyway because External Secrets reconciles the mirror (20s refresh interval) once the source exists — but it means Traefik's env is momentarily unsatisfiable mid-deploy by design. Details on the Data & secrets page.

The same ordering is encoded twice: imperatively in deploy:_apply for task deploys, and declaratively as per-component healthChecks in the Zarf package (below), which waits on the same deployments between components.

Local environment: kind

task up creates a kind cluster named opendefence-kind (node image kindest/node:v1.35.1, single control-plane node) from kind-config.yaml, waits for the node, then runs deploy:local. The kind config does three things:

  • Widens the NodePort range (service-node-port-range: 1024-9999) so raw TCP/UDP services that bypass Traefik — TAK streaming, MediaMTX media, LiveKit — can be exposed as NodePort services on their real port numbers.
  • Maps host ports into the node via extraPortMappings, summarized:
Host ports Bind Purpose
80, 443 127.0.0.1/TCP Traefik web / websecure entrypoints
9443 127.0.0.1/TCP Keycloak's own TLS listener
8089, 8090–8094, 8443, 9000–9002 127.0.0.1/TCP TAK: CoT streaming, data feeds, native HTTPS, federation
1936, 8322, 8890 (TCP+UDP), 9888, 9889 0.0.0.0 MediaMTX: RTMPS, RTSPS, SRT, HLS, WebRTC — bound on all interfaces so LAN devices can stream
9996–9999 127.0.0.1/TCP MediaMTX playback, control API, metrics, pprof
7881/TCP, 7882/UDP, 3478/UDP, 5349/TCP 0.0.0.0 LiveKit (MatrixRTC): ICE, media, TURN, TURN-TLS
  • Labels the node **ingress-ready=true**; the local Traefik overlay (k8s/traefik/overlays/local/patch-traefik.yaml) runs Traefik with hostNetwork: true and hostPort 80/443, so the entrypoints sit directly on the node and line up with the port mappings. (Cloud uses the chart's default exposure instead.)

Before applying any phase, deploy:local runs the coredns:local task — the piece that makes the local cluster behave like a real deployment. The public DNS record for localmaeher.dev.pvarki.fi points at 127.0.0.1, which is correct for a browser on the developer's machine but useless inside a pod, where 127.0.0.1 is the pod itself. The task patches the coredns ConfigMap in kube-system with a CoreDNS template plugin block that answers any A query under localmaeher.dev.pvarki.fi with the kind node's InternalIP (and returns empty NOERROR for AAAA), then restarts CoreDNS.

The payoff: when an in-cluster pod calls a public URL — for example an integration container fetching from https://mtls.localmaeher.dev.pvarki.fi — the request resolves to the node, enters Traefik through the real websecure entrypoint, and gets the full edge treatment: the real server certificate, client-certificate verification against the internal CA, and the callsign middleware chain (see Edge mTLS & callsign checks). Edge mTLS is therefore exercised identically from inside and outside the cluster, instead of being short-circuited through cluster-internal Services:

blocks.html:
Cloud environment: k3s + Zarf

The cloud target is a single k3s VM (Azure in current practice). There are two ways to reach it. task deploy:cloud runs the exact same phased apply as local, just with --kubeconfig k3s-azure.yaml and the k8s/main/cloud entry points. The packaged path is Zarf: task zarf:package:cloud builds a self-contained deployment artifact from zarf/cloud/zarf.template.yaml.

Cloud overlays never hardcode a hostname. Every host-dependent value is written as the Zarf token ###ZARF_VAR_OPENDEFENCE_HOST### (certificates, IngressRoutes, well-known files, kraftwerk configs), replaced at zarf package deploy time from the OPENDEFENCE_HOST variable, which the package prompts for if not passed with --set. A second variable, OPENDEFENCE_DEPLOYMENT, is derived automatically by an onDeploy action — echo "$ZARF_VAR_OPENDEFENCE_HOST" | cut -d. -f1 — and feeds tokens like the PKI's "###ZARF_VAR_OPENDEFENCE_DEPLOYMENT### Root CA" common name. One package artifact therefore serves any deployment; the identity is injected at deploy time.

The build renders each cloud phase with kubectl kustomize --enable-helm into static manifests (phase 1 rendered per bundles/* entry, as above), copies the template to .build/zarf/cloud/zarf.yaml, stamps in the version, and produces one of two flavors:

  • Online ("YOLO") — ZARF_YOLO=true sets metadata.yolo: true and strips all component images lists. No images are embedded; the target cluster pulls them from their original registries. Small artifact, needs internet on the cluster.
  • Offline-full — zarf dev find-images --update scans the rendered manifests and embeds every image in the package (the build manually appends ghcr.io/cloudnative-pg/postgresql:18.0-system-trixie, which CNPG init jobs reference dynamically and image discovery misses). This is the air-gap artifact: the cluster needs no registry access at all.

CI publishes both flavors of every release as OCI artifacts:

Each published package is keyless-signed with cosign using the GitHub Actions OIDC identity (cosign signs the resolved digest, not the tag; zarf/cloud/README.md in the repo has the verify one-liner). The package's components mirror the taskfile's phase gates as Zarf healthChecks — the deploy waits on the same deployments (cnpg-controller-manager, cert-manager-webhook, the ESO pair, trust-manager, the three Linkerd deployments, rmapi, keycloak) between components:

blocks.html:
Versioning: CalVer, and no GitOps

Releases are calendar-versioned as YYYY.MM.patch (e.g. 2026.06.1), with the arithmetic owned by bump-my-version. The flow is fully automatic: every push to main triggers .github/workflows/tag.yml, which computes the next CalVer from the latest existing tag (seeding from YYYY.MM.0 when no tag exists yet) and pushes a vYYYY.MM.patch git tag — no version-bump commits, no commit-message conventions. The tag push triggers .github/workflows/release.yml, which validates the tag shape, builds both Zarf flavors at that commit, publishes and cosign-signs them on GHCR, and creates a GitHub Release. Only the online package is attached to the Release as an asset; the offline-full package (with every image embedded) is pulled from GHCR.

Just as important is what the platform does not have: there is no GitOps. No Argo CD, no Flux, no in-cluster agent reconciling the cluster against the repo. State reaches the cluster only when someone runs task deploy:local, task deploy:cloud, or zarf package deploy. Consequences to be aware of:

  • Nothing detects or corrects drift between the repo and the cluster.
  • kubectl apply --server-side without pruning means resources removed from the repo are not removed from the cluster — cleanup is manual.
  • "What version is running" is answered by what was last applied, not by anything the cluster reports against a desired state.

This is a deliberate simplicity trade-off for the closed alpha, not an accident — but plan operations around it (see Day-2 operations (Kubernetes)).

Developer tooling

For iterating on this stack you rarely run the full phase pipeline repeatedly. The repo documents DevSpace for live-editing workloads, and mirrord is the standard way to run a local core-API process against a real cluster. Both are covered in their own guides: Set up your dev environment (Kubernetes) and Iterate on the core API with mirrord.
